--- page 1 ---
Week 4: Attention and Memory
This week we look at how attention shapes what we remember.
Attention acts as a filter that decides which parts of the world reach awareness.
Information that is never attended to is rarely stored for long.
Psychologists have long argued that memory depends on selective attention to the right details at the right moment.
When attention is divided, people encode less and later recall fewer of the items they saw.
Working memory capacity is limited to a few items at once.
Most adults can hold about four chunks of information in mind.
--- page 2 ---
Attention is often compared to a spotlight that moves across a scene.
Objects inside the spotlight are processed quickly and in detail.
Objects outside it are processed slowly, if at all.
A second view treats attention as a limited pool of resources.
Hard tasks draw heavily on the pool and leave little for anything else.
This explains why talking on the phone makes driving more dangerous.
--- page 3 ---
Memory researchers separate encoding, storage and retrieval.
Encoding turns an experience into a lasting trace.
Storage keeps the trace over time, and retrieval brings it back when it is needed.
Each stage can fail on its own.
A student who never encoded a fact cannot retrieve it, no matter how hard they try.
A student who encoded it well may still fail to retrieve it under stress.
--- page 4 ---
Practice testing is one of the most reliable ways to improve retrieval.
Each attempt to recall strengthens the path back to the memory.
Spacing practice over several days works better than cramming the night before.
Next week we turn to long-term memory and the ways it can be distorted.
